sections.markdown:
## C — The basics, part one: pre-drive checks, who yields, the four-second rule and speed limits, merging, intersections, stopping, sight distance and the space around your vehicle
Knowledge domain: the everyday rules of control and courtesy that Wisconsin tests most often — getting ready to drive, deciding who goes first, choosing a safe speed, entering and leaving traffic, handling intersections and railroad crossings, stopping smoothly and keeping a space cushion in front, behind and to the sides.

FACT_ID: sec03-F01 | anchor: A01
Before driving, make sure you carry your valid driver license, proof of insurance and the vehicle registration, and check that the car is in good working order. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-F02 | anchor: A01
Before moving, buckle your own seat belt, see that every passenger is buckled, and adjust the seat and mirrors so you can see out of every window. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-F03 | anchor: A01
Right-of-way decides who proceeds first and who waits, especially where drivers or pedestrians meet without signals or signs, and you should never assume the vehicle on the right automatically goes first. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-F04 | anchor: A01
Whatever the situation, you are always required to yield when that is needed to avoid striking a pedestrian, a bicyclist or another vehicle. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-F05 | anchor: A01
Yield to pedestrians, bicyclists and drivers who are still in the intersection. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-F06 | anchor: A01
At a four-way stop the first driver or bicyclist to arrive goes first, and when two or more arrive together the driver on the right goes first. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-F07 | anchor: A01
At an uncontrolled intersection with no signs or signals, yield to vehicles approaching from your right. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-F08 | anchor: A01
Yield to traffic already circulating in a roundabout, and to cross traffic at an uncontrolled T-intersection. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-F09 | anchor: A01
Yield to a pedestrian who uses a guide dog or carries a white cane even if that person is not in the intersection, stopping at least ten feet away until the person has left the roadway. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-F10 | anchor: A01
Yield to a vehicle passing you on either side in your direction, to oncoming vehicles when you turn left or make a U-turn, and to emergency vehicles using lights or sirens. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-F11 | anchor: A02
Choose a speed that always leaves you able to stop safely, and measure your gap with the Four Second Following Distance Rule. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-F12 | anchor: A02
To apply the four-second rule, pick a fixed object ahead such as a tree, sign or house and count from one thousand one to one thousand four; reaching the object before you finish means you are going too fast. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-F13 | anchor: A02
Add one extra second to the following count for each adverse condition, such as heavier traffic, rain, snow or ice. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-F14 | anchor: A02
A speed limit is the highest legal speed for the area, exceeding the posted limit is illegal, and you may not speed up past the limit to pass another vehicle. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-F15 | anchor: A02
Racing and reckless driving are illegal, so keep scanning the roadside for the posted speed limit sign. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-F16 | anchor: A02
Unless a sign says otherwise, the speed limit in residential areas is 25 mph. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-F17 | anchor: A02
The usual school zone limit when children are present is 15 mph. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-F18 | anchor: A02
In the outlying parts of cities and villages where no limit is posted, the maximum is 35 mph. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-F19 | anchor: A02
The limit is a maximum, so poor visibility or road conditions may call for a slower speed. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-F20 | anchor: A02
Driving either too fast or too slow can cause a crash, because slow drivers make traffic stack up behind them, and police can ticket you for either. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-F21 | anchor: A02
If you drive slower than most traffic on a multi-lane road, use the far-right lane. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-F22 | anchor: A02
Try to match the speed of surrounding traffic, and when merging, enter at the speed the traffic is moving without forcing anyone to brake or swerve. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-F23 | anchor: A02
On a highway you use the acceleration lane of the on-ramp to build speed as you merge, and finding a safe, legal gap is your responsibility. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-F24 | anchor: A02
When leaving a highway, move into the deceleration lane of the off-ramp and slow down gradually there, checking around you as you leave traffic. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-F25 | anchor: A03
The faster you travel, the more distance you need to turn, slow down or stop, so adjust speed to road and traffic conditions. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0015]

FACT_ID: sec03-F26 | anchor: A03
For good control you need to see 10 to 15 seconds ahead of your vehicle. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0015]

FACT_ID: sec03-F27 | anchor: A03
Slow down on curves and hills, when rain, snow or hail begins, in parking lots, malls and downtown areas, near schools, playgrounds and residential streets, and in heavy traffic; avoid driving at all on icy roads if you can. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0015]

FACT_ID: sec03-F28 | anchor: A03
An intersection is any place where two paths cross, which includes cross streets, driveways, parking lot entrances and railroad crossings. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0015]

FACT_ID: sec03-F29 | anchor: A03
Before entering an intersection, look left and right, make sure no vehicles or pedestrians are in it, and check for a clear path to where you are going. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0015]

FACT_ID: sec03-F30 | anchor: A03
If you cannot see well into an intersection, edge forward carefully and stay ready to brake, especially where there are no signals or signs. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0015]

FACT_ID: sec03-F31 | anchor: A03
Trees, buildings and parked vehicles can hide cross traffic, so approach a blocked intersection slowly. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0015]

FACT_ID: sec03-F32 | anchor: A03
Because some drivers miss or ignore signs and signals, search left, right and left again before crossing, even when you have the right-of-way. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0015]

FACT_ID: sec03-F33 | anchor: A04
Watching far ahead lets you begin slowing early, because a sudden stop can make you lose control or get you rear-ended, while early braking gives a gradual, safer stop. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0016]

FACT_ID: sec03-F34 | anchor: A04
Do not coast in neutral; keep the car in gear so you have full control. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0016]

FACT_ID: sec03-F35 | anchor: A04
The sight distance rule says that when your view ahead is shorter than 10 to 15 seconds of travel, you are required to reduce speed. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0016]

FACT_ID: sec03-F36 | anchor: A04
Check all your mirrors while driving, looking left, right, ahead and behind with the rearview mirror. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0016]

FACT_ID: sec03-F37 | anchor: A04
At a railroad crossing never assume no train is coming: stop before the crossing, look both ways, listen, and make sure there is room for your car on the far side. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0016]

FACT_ID: sec03-F38 | anchor: A04
Do not stare at drivers who have been pulled over or at other roadside activity, because that distraction can cause a crash. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0016]

FACT_ID: sec03-F39 | anchor: A04
Keep space on every side of your car, give large vehicles extra room so you can see around them and they can see you, and move ahead of or behind a vehicle riding right beside you when safe. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0016]

FACT_ID: sec03-F40 | anchor: A04
For space in front, apply the four-second following distance rule whenever you are behind another vehicle. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0016]

FACT_ID: sec03-F41 | anchor: A05
Leave more than four seconds ahead on slippery, icy or snowy roads, when the driver behind wants to pass, and when following trucks, buses, vans, large vehicles, motorcycles or bicycles. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0017]

FACT_ID: sec03-F42 | anchor: A05
Also leave extra following time when hauling a heavy load or trailer, when someone is tailgating you, when emergency vehicles are ahead, at railroad crossings, and when stopping on a hill. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0017]

FACT_ID: sec03-F43 | anchor: A05
Check the rearview mirror every 6 to 8 seconds for tailgaters, and if someone is following too closely, slow down gradually to encourage them to pass. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0017]

FACT_ID: sec03-F44 | anchor: A05
Help drivers behind you by holding a steady speed and signaling well before you slow or turn, and give extra room to a driver who cannot see behind their own vehicle. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0017]

FACT_ID: sec03-F45 | anchor: A05
To pick up or drop off passengers, find a safe spot out of traffic; if you are slower than most traffic on a multi-lane road, keep right and pull over so others can pass on the left. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0017]

FACT_ID: sec03-F46 | anchor: A05
Before crossing traffic or a multi-lane road, make sure there is room to clear it completely, check for vehicles and pedestrians, and wait until it is safe. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0017]

Misconceptions: the vehicle on the right does not always go first, since arrival order decides at a four-way stop; having the right-of-way does not excuse you from searching left, right and left again; driving slowly is not automatically safe, because it can also cause crashes and tickets; the posted limit is a ceiling, not a target, in poor conditions; a white cane or guide dog user gets the right-of-way even outside the intersection.
Mnemonics: count one thousand one through one thousand four for the gap and add a second per hazard; twenty-five for homes, fifteen for schools with children, thirty-five for the edge of town; look ten to fifteen seconds ahead and check behind every six to eight; left, right, left before you go.
Glossary: right-of-way means the rule for who goes first and who waits; uncontrolled intersection means one with no signs or signals; four-way stop means an intersection where all directions stop; acceleration lane means the on-ramp lane used to reach traffic speed; deceleration lane means the off-ramp lane used to slow down; coasting means rolling in neutral; tailgating means following too closely.
Dynamic facts: posted speed limits vary by road and can change, so the default residential, school zone and outlying limits apply only where no other limit is posted.
